title: The 5 Biggest Craters in the Solar System, Ranked (Earth Isn't Close)

scenes.text: The five biggest impact craters in the solar system. Four of them are on one planet.
Number five: Argyre, on Mars. About 1,700 kilometres across, its floor 5 kilometres below the surrounding plains.
scenes.label: Argyre · 1,700 km

scenes.text: Number four: Isidis, Mars again. About 1,900 kilometres wide. Europe's Beagle 2 lander vanished here in 2003, found in 2015.
scenes.label: Isidis · 1,900 km

scenes.text: Number three: Hellas, Mars. 2,300 kilometres wide and over 7 deep, the lowest ground on the planet.
scenes.label: Hellas · 2,300 km

scenes.text: Number two: South Pole-Aitken, on the far side of the Moon. 2,500 kilometres across and more than 8 deep.
scenes.label: South Pole-Aitken · 2,500 km

scenes.text: Number one: Utopia, Mars, about 3,300 kilometres across, with enough buried ice to fill Lake Superior. Earth's biggest, Vredefort, is 300. Not close.
scenes.label: Utopia · 3,300 km

description:
The five largest confirmed impact basins in the solar system, ranked by diameter.
Argyre on Mars is about 1,700 kilometres wide with a floor 5.2 kilometres below the surrounding plains; Isidis, also on Mars, is about 1,900 kilometres across and was the landing site where ESA's Beagle 2 went silent in 2003 before being spotted on the surface in 2015; Hellas is 2,300 kilometres wide and more than 7 kilometres deep, holding the lowest elevations on Mars; the Moon's South Pole-Aitken basin is roughly 2,500 kilometres across and more than 8 kilometres deep; and Utopia Planitia on Mars is about 3,300 kilometres across, with a buried ice deposit holding as much water as Lake Superior. Earth's largest confirmed crater, Vredefort in South Africa, was originally 180 to 300 kilometres wide.
Which crater would you want to stand inside?
first_comment: Which would you put at number one? Mars may hide an even bigger one: the unconfirmed Borealis basin would be 8,500 kilometres across. What should we rank next?
